analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicare rebates when prices outpace inflation and lowers seniors' drug costs.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee reported this drug-pricing bill in September 2019 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets prescription drug prices in Medicare and Medicaid. It makes drug manufacturers pay rebates when prices of Medicare-covered drugs rise faster than inflation, and refund Medicare for drug left over in single-dose vials that providers throw away. It redesigns the Medicare drug benefit so seniors pay nothing out of pocket after reaching a roughly $3,100 annual cap, with drug makers footing much of the bill through a new discount program, and it forces pharmacy benefit managers to disclose their rebate deals and bans 'spread pricing' in Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries get a lower annual out-of-pocket cap (set at $3,100 in 2022) and no cost sharing above it, funded largely by manufacturer discounts at the pharmacy counter [S4]. Taxpayers gain because inflation rebates and discarded-drug refunds go into the Medicare trust fund [S4]. State Medicaid programs gain from higher manufacturer rebates and the end of spread pricing, a middleman practice that inflates what states pay for drugs [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare for single-source drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation, with the money deposited into the Medicare trust fund [S4].
Requires manufacturers to refund Medicare for the portion of single-dose vial drugs that providers discard, ending a practice where patients and taxpayers paid for unused medicine [S2] [S4].

Redesigns the Medicare Part D benefit so the annual out-of-pocket threshold drops to $3,100 in 2022 and beneficiaries pay nothing above it, with manufacturers providing discounted prices (80% of the negotiated price) for drugs dispensed above that threshold [S4].

Bars spread pricing in Medicaid — the practice where pharmacy benefit managers charge states more than they pay pharmacies and keep the difference — and requires public disclosure of drug discounts and rebate arrangements [S2].

Increases the maximum rebate drug manufacturers owe under the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and requires CMS to publish information reported by PBMs about discounts and payments among PBMs, health plans, and pharmacies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the main cost: inflation-linked rebates, refunds for discarded doses, a higher Medicaid rebate cap, and an 80% discount on Part D drugs dispensed above the out-of-pocket cap [S2] [S4]. Pharmacy benefit managers lose revenue and face new public disclosure of their rebate deals [S2]. Prescription drug plans see federal reinsurance for catastrophic cases shrink, though manufacturer discounts offset much of the added liability [S4].

drawbacks.text: The Part D redesign depends on manufacturers voluntarily maintaining discount agreements, and the bill's text lets a manufacturer terminate its agreement 'for any reason' with about a year's notice, which could disrupt the benefit if a major drug maker walks away [S4].

The inflation rebate penalizes only single-source drugs, so it does nothing about generic competition, and industry argued such rebates would reduce investment in new medicines — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, since Medicare Part B relies heavily on newer biologics.
The bill requires extensive new price-reporting and data systems from manufacturers, plans, and pharmacies, and its studies and pilots add administrative burden without guaranteeing savings [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors and taxpayers, the benefits are concrete: a firm out-of-pocket cap, no cost sharing above it, and rebates when prices outrun inflation. The design is heavier on transparency and reporting than on direct price negotiation, so savings depend on manufacturers and PBMs actually complying, and the discount program has a structural weakness — manufacturers can exit it. Still, the bill's costs fall mostly on manufacturers and middlemen, not on patients, and it was considered serious, bipartisan legislation rather than a throwaway.

outcome.mechanism: The Finance Committee reported the bill and it sat on the Senate calendar for over a year, but the majority leader never brought it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley, the Finance Committee chairman, introduced the bill as an original committee measure and it was reported to the Senate with written report No. 116-120 on September 25, 2019 [S6].
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 225 — the queue for bills awaiting a floor vote [S6] [S4].
The bill had zero cosponsors, which is typical for an original committee measure drafted by the chairman and ranking member [S5].
No further action followed: the bill never received a Senate floor vote, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing it [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they never had to pay the inflation rebates, discarded-drug refunds, higher Medicaid rebates, or the 80% point-of-sale discounts the bill would have imposed. Pharmacy benefit managers also avoided the spread-pricing ban and rebate disclosure.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as an original Finance Committee measure, reported it to the Senate with written report No. 116-120, and had it placed on the Senate calendar

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Worked with Grassley across party lines to draft the bill through the Finance Committee

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote despite it sitting on the legislative calendar for more than a year

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the inflation-rebate and out-of-pocket redesign provisions and ran ad campaigns criticizing Senate drug-pricing proposals

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Pressed Senate Republicans for a drug-pricing bill, then cooled on Grassley's approach as negotiations with House Speaker Pelosi over a competing House bill dragged on

sides.party_line_note: The bill was developed by a Republican committee chairman and the Democratic ranking member, but it never reached a floor vote, so the Senate never recorded a party-line roll call on it.

industries.note: The bill hits makers of single-source brand drugs from several angles: rebates when prices rise faster than inflation, refunds for discarded single-dose vials, a higher Medicaid rebate cap, and an 80% discount on Medicare Part D drugs dispensed above the out-of-pocket cap. The bill died, so these obligations never took effect.

The bill requires public disclosure of PBM rebate and discount arrangements and bans spread pricing in Medicaid, where PBMs pocket the gap between what states pay and what pharmacies receive. The bill died, so these rules never took effect.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plans
industries.note: The redesign cuts the federal reinsurance share of catastrophic drug costs, shifting more risk onto plans, but manufacturers must supply discounts covering 80% of negotiated prices above the out-of-pocket cap, largely offsetting that. Beneficiaries come out clearly ahead with the new $3,100 cap.
